steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the "Method" section of an encyclopedia article on amortized analysis: what the technique needs in order to apply, and a short description of each of the standard methods for doing it.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- What amortized analysis requires
- Basic idea: a worst-case operation pays off over time
- The three methods
- Aggregate method
- Accounting method
- Potential method

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Requirements
  - need to know which series of operations are possible
  - most common with data structures: state persists between operations
- Basic idea
  - worst-case op can alter state so worst case can't occur again for a long time
  - "amortizing" its cost
- Three methods
  - aggregate, accounting, potential
  - all give correct answers; pick whichever is most convenient for the situation
- Aggregate
  - upper bound T(n) on total cost of sequence of n operations
  - amortized cost = T(n) / n
- Accounting
  - form of aggregate analysis; each op gets amortized cost, may differ from actual cost
  - early ops: amortized > actual -> saved "credit"; pays for later ops with amortized < actual
  - credit starts at zero -> actual cost = amortized cost minus accumulated credit
  - credit non-negative -> amortized cost is upper bound on actual cost
  - many short-running ops build credit in small increments; rare long-running ops decrease it drastically
- Potential
  - form of accounting method; saved credit computed as function ("potential") of data structure state
  - amortized cost = immediate cost + change in potential

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
To do amortized analysis you need to know which series of operations are possible. Usually this is the case with data structures, because they have a state that stays around between operations. The basic idea is that an operation that is a worst case can change the state so that the worst case can't happen again for a long time, and so its cost gets "amortized".

There are generally three methods for doing amortized analysis. They are the aggregate method, the accounting method, and the potential method. All of them give correct answers, and which one you use just depends on which one is most convenient for the situation.

The aggregate analysis finds the upper bound T(n) on the total cost of a sequence of n operations. Then the amortized cost is calculated as T(n) / n.

- Accounting method
  - kind of aggregate analysis; each op gets an amortized cost that may differ from actual cost
  - early ops amortized > actual, builds saved "credit"; pays for later ops with amortized < actual
  - credit starts at zero -> actual cost = amortized cost minus accumulated credit
  - credit non-negative -> amortized cost is an upper bound on actual cost
  - many short-running ops add credit in small increments, rare long-running ops decrease it drastically
- Potential method
  - kind of accounting method; saved credit = function ("potential") of data structure state
  - amortized cost = immediate cost + change in potential

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
To do amortized analysis you need to know which series of operations are possible. Usually this is the case with data structures, because they have a state that stays around between operations. The basic idea is that an operation that is a worst case can change the state so that the worst case can't happen again for a long time, and so its cost gets "amortized".

There are generally three methods for doing amortized analysis. They are the aggregate method, the accounting method, and the potential method. All of them give correct answers, and which one you use just depends on which one is most convenient for the situation.

The aggregate analysis finds the upper bound T(n) on the total cost of a sequence of n operations. Then the amortized cost is calculated as T(n) / n.

The accounting method is a kind of aggregate analysis. It gives each operation an amortized cost, and this cost can be different from the actual cost. The early operations get an amortized cost that is higher than their actual cost, and this builds up a saved "credit". The credit then pays for later operations that have an amortized cost lower than their actual cost. The credit starts at zero, so the actual cost of a sequence of operations is the amortized cost minus the credit that was accumulated. The credit has to be non-negative, so the amortized cost is an upper bound on the actual cost. Usually there are many short-running operations that build up the credit in small increments, and there are rare long-running operations that decrease it a lot.

The potential method is a kind of accounting method where the saved credit is computed as a function of the state of the data structure, which is called the "potential". The amortized cost is the immediate cost plus the change in potential.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Amortized analysis requires knowing which series of operations are possible. This is most commonly the case with data structures, which have a state that persists between operations. The basic idea is that a worst-case operation can change the state in such a way that the worst case cannot occur again for a long time, thus "amortizing" its cost.

There are generally three methods for performing amortized analysis: the aggregate method, the accounting method, and the potential method. All of them give correct answers; which one to use depends on which is most convenient for a particular situation.[1]

Aggregate analysis determines the upper bound T(n) on the total cost of a sequence of n operations, and then calculates the amortized cost as T(n) / n.[1]

The accounting method is a form of aggregate analysis which assigns each operation an amortized cost that may differ from its actual cost. Early operations have an amortized cost higher than their actual cost, which accumulates a saved "credit" that pays for later operations whose amortized cost is lower than their actual cost. Since the credit begins at zero, the actual cost of a sequence of operations equals the amortized cost minus the accumulated credit, and since the credit must be non-negative, the amortized cost is an upper bound on the actual cost. Usually, many short-running operations accumulate this credit in small increments, while rare long-running operations decrease it drastically.[1]

The potential method is a form of the accounting method in which the saved credit is computed as a function (the "potential") of the state of the data structure. The amortized cost is then the immediate cost plus the change in potential.[1]

References:
[1] Kozen, Dexter. (Spring 2011). CS 3110 Lecture 20: Amortized Analysis. Cornell University. https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs3110/2011sp/lectures/lec20-amortized/amortized.htm
